summary: A web project adds many users, a network, shared data, untrusted input and deployment to the concerns of Project I.
ClinicQ is the running example; its objectives are measurable and its scope table lists what is out.
The three-tier architecture separates the browser, the logic and the database; every arrow between them is a trust boundary.
REST uses nouns for URLs, verbs for actions and status codes for the outcome.
Choose the stack for the team's skills; this book uses the Python standard library to show the mechanics.

sections.title: Designing the data
What happens when a request arrives
The ClinicQ API, complete
Two clerks at the same moment: the race condition
Transactions and error replies
Eight reasons to validate and constrain at every layer

summary: ClinicQ has two tables, patient and token, in a one-to-many relation with five kinds of constraint.
A request flows: parse, validate, run SQL, build JSON, reply; invalid input is rejected early.
The 78-line API replies 201, 400, 404, 422 and 200 and was run over a real local HTTP connection.
Race conditions are solved by database constraints plus a retry, not by hoping.
Safe errors tell the client what to fix and hide the internals.

sections.title: Who are you, and what may you do?

SQL injection: the attack and the cure
Brute force and rate limiting

Eight security practices every student web project needs

summary: Authentication and authorisation are different questions with different status codes.
Passwords are stored as salted slow hashes; the run showed different hashes for one password and a failed check for one changed letter.
Signed tokens carry user, role and expiry; the run refused edited, expired and malformed tokens.
Parameterised SQL beats injection; rate limits and long passwords beat brute force.
Security is layered: HTTPS, login and roles, validation, protected data and logs.

summary: Tests are layered; the 9-test suite for ClinicQ rules passed and each test name states a requirement.
The test-case table with expected and actual results is the evidence the examiner reads.
Capacity is computed: at peak ClinicQ needs about 4 requests per second, 16 % of one small worker.
A cache and more workers are the first scaling steps.
Deployment is a repeatable pipeline with a health check; Nginx handles HTTPS and systemd keeps the service alive.

summary: The report proves every early claim with evidence in later chapters.
Generated API documentation and a good README let a stranger use the system.
A timed demo with a fallback survives load-shedding and network failures.
Twelve viva questions cover architecture, REST, security, concurrency, testing and deployment.
Honesty, numbers and shared understanding are what separate good projects from copied ones.
